I'm planning out a TypeScript module for a Warcraft-style dwarf blacksmith at an anvil, with chunky proportions, pauldrons, a braided beard, and rigged joints for a humanoid figure, aiming for a robust but manageable module size.

I'm settling on model-space absolute coordinates to avoid confusion with local joint orientation. For the dwarf's design, I'm leaning toward a Bronzebeard-style look: bald head with bushy brows, a thick red-orange braided beard with metal rings, a mustache, and maybe goggles pushed up on the forehead for an engineer vibe rather than a helmet.

Now I'm working out body proportions with feet at y=0, chunky boots, and leg joint positions using inverse kinematics to place hips, knees, and ankles at the right heights and depths.

For the torso, I'm planning a dwarf's wide, barrel-shaped build using a loft technique along a spine bone chain, defining cross-section stations from hips to neck with varying widths and heights to capture the belly and broad chest.

Now I'm working out the spine chain itself - plotting three points from hips through torso to neck base with a slight forward curve, and figuring out how the joint naming needs to match the number of spans created by the catmull interpolation between those points.

To reduce risk, maybe I should use rigid parts explicitly tied to the spine bone instead of a loft, though that'd be less smooth. Since I can't fully verify SDK behavior, I'll keep the loft but anchor it to the spine chain alone, starting the chain lower at the pelvis so the joint position and loft start align properly.

Adding a pelvis sphere on the hips bone to cover the area below the loft start, then defining the spine loft with catmull-interpolated stations rising from hips to the upper torso, split into three named spine segments.

The last spine joint's span covers 0.9 to 1.04, so that gives the neck its parent anchor. Now for the head, I'm placing a joint near the top of the neck and deciding how to orient its direction—leaning toward just using absolute model-space coordinates for the head rather than local joint-relative ones to keep things simpler.

For the dwarf's head itself, I'm making it big and chunky relative to the body: a head center around (0, 1.27, 0.06), built from a stretched sphere for the cranium, a brow ridge box, a large ruddy nose, cheek spheres, and pointy ears.

For the eyes, I'm deciding between simple geometric parts (white sphere plus dark pupil) or painted decals on the skull surface using a raycast to find the exact placement point on the face, leaning toward decals for a cleaner painted look.

I'll design the eye decal as a small SVG with a white almond shape, blue-grey iris, dark pupil, highlight, and upper lid line, sized to sit under a heavy brow. For the beard, I'm planning a loft shape hanging from the chin down toward the belly, tapering in width and height as it descends.

Thinking about attachment points, I realize attaching the beard mass to the jaw rather than the head makes more sense since it would move naturally with mouth motion, even if it clips slightly when opening. I'll build the lower jaw as its own part with a chin block and lower lip, mostly concealed by the mustache and beard above it.

For the beard texture itself, I'm planning a custom paint function mixing dark auburn and orange tones using noise-based strand patterns oriented along the vertical axis, blending from root to tip for a natural fur look.

Now I'm adding braids hanging from the sides—chains of linked spheroids following a path with alternating tilt, capped with small metal ring clasps. I'm also scattering fluffy tuft cards across the beard surface using flame-like orange textures, keeping the count modest (around 50) for a wispy fringe effect without overloading the scene.

For the mustache, I'm sweeping curved tubes from the nose down each side with end swirls, mirrored symmetrically. Then for hair, I'm considering a mohawk-style crest made of overlapping flame-shaped extrudes running front-to-back along the head, paired with forehead goggles and a strap, going for that stout dwarven warrior look.

Placing goggle lenses as brass-rimmed cylinders angled upward on the forehead, then sizing out the skull sphere's proportions.

Working out the facial geometry further: jaw and cheek spheres, a small nose, angled brow capsules, ruddy cheekbone spheres, and eye positions along the brow line.

Now I'm figuring out the skull surface math to place eye decals correctly at the right depth, then moving to ears -- planning pointy cone or extruded ear shapes angled outward from the sides of the head.

Next I'm working out a warm ruddy skin tone with mottled cheeks, planning to define a base skin color variable to build from.

For the mouth area, since the mustache covers most of it, I'm sketching a simple jaw: a chin block, a small dark mouth interior hidden beneath the facial hair, and a lower lip piece, keeping the upper jaw handled separately by the head geometry.

Now I'm moving to the jaw joint attachment and beginning the leather apron for the torso—planning an extruded bib-shaped panel that sits over the protruding belly, narrower at top and wider at bottom.

I'm working out the tilt of the apron's extrusion direction so the bottom tucks closer to the body while the top sits further out, trying to figure out whether the direction vector needs to be normalized before computing the cross product for the outline plane.

Now I'm fine-tuning the apron placement so it clips correctly against the torso loft, nudging its position and thickness slightly. Defining more stations...

Going with Ironforge-inspired colors: a dark blue tunic with bronze pauldrons, brown leather apron, and orange beard to fit the dwarf blacksmith theme. Deciding the model's right hand holds the hammer while the left holds tongs gripping a billet, with both arms bent forward toward the anvil at z=0.62, hands positioned slightly outside and in front around (s*0.33, 0.78, 0.38), hammer pointed upward in the right hand.
